cues.text: The origin of energy production and biosynthesis inside your living cells is the dynamic mitochondria organelle.

Mitochondria are filled with metabolic enzymes that catalyze a loop of chemical reactions called the citric acid cycle. The eight steps of the citric acid cycle gradually break apart two carbon atoms from glucose, capturing liberated electrons for the electron transport chain while generating carbon dioxide as waste.
The citric acid cycle starts with the end product of a previous cycle: the four-carbon molecule oxaloacetate.
New carbon enters from glycolysis in the form of acetyl-CoA, a two-carbon acetyl group attached to coenzyme A.
Step One is the catalytic transfer of a two-carbon acetyl group from coenzyme A to four-carbon oxaloacetate, creating six-carbon citric acid — the molecule that gives the cycle its name.
Citric acid is used by your cells for the biosynthesis of fatty acids, lipids, and cholesterol, and is also the substrate for step two of the citric acid cycle.
The enzyme reaction of step two makes a small change to the citric acid molecule, moving the position of an oxygen atom, converting citrate into isocitrate.
Step three of the cycle removes a carbon atom, forming carbon dioxide as waste while converting six-carbon isocitrate to five-carbon alpha-ketoglutarate.
During this process, chemical energy is harvested when two electrons are transferred to coenzyme NADH, which delivers them to nearby enzymes of the electron transport chain.

Step four of the citric acid cycle is performed by a huge multi-enzyme complex connecting multiple chemical reactions with flexible tethers, efficiently moving reactants between active sites and diverting electrons between pathways.

The large complex is made with a repeating unit of three core enzymes working in sequence to remove a carbon atom from ketoglutarate, generating carbon dioxide waste then attaching four-carbon succinyl to coenzyme A.
The electron from ketoglutarate oxidation is retained by the tethered enzyme before passing it to coenzyme NADH, which delivers electrons to the electron transport chain.
Enzymes of step five separate succinyl from coenzyme A by breaking an energetic bond, providing enough energy to create GTP.

GTP is a building block of RNA and an energy source for protein synthesis in the most direct path to ATP from the citric acid cycle. Other enzymes in the matrix can use GTP to make the chemical fuel ATP.
Step six is performed by an enzyme embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane. This enzyme is also known as Complex II of the electron transport chain.
The enzyme catalyzes the oxidation of succinate to create fumarate, releasing two electrons that hop through the interior to coenzyme Q, which is reduced.
Coenzyme Q travels in the membrane carrying the electrons to nearby enzymes of the electron transport chain.
Step seven takes fumarate generated by step six and reacts it with water to create four-carbon malate.
The final step of the citric acid cycle uses malate to regenerate oxaloacetate, transferring electrons to coenzyme NADH, which supplies the electron transport chain.
Oxaloacetate can return to step one for another loop of the cycle and is also an essential building block for making amino acids and the genetic code of DNA and RNA.
At the center of cellular metabolism, the citric acid cycle generates both chemical energy and material for biosynthesis of the entire diversity of molecules found inside a living cell.
The cycle runs in the mitochondrial matrix, the fluid inside the inner membrane. Everything you are about to watch is dissolved enzymes bumping into substrates.
Eight steps in a loop. Watch the carbon count rather than the names: 4 → 6 → 5 → 4, and the two that leave do so as CO₂. That is the carbon you breathe out.
It starts where it ended. Oxaloacetate is not consumed by the cycle, it is regenerated by it, which is what makes this a cycle and not a pathway.
Acetyl-CoA is the only way carbon gets in. Glycolysis handed over pyruvate; pyruvate oxidation stripped one carbon and tied the other two to coenzyme A.
Two carbons in, joined to four, making six. Citrate synthase closes its two halves around the pair, which is why the reaction only runs one way.
The cycle is not only a furnace. Citrate leaving the mitochondrion is where the carbon in your body fat comes from — the same molecule, spent on building instead of burning.
A hydroxyl moves one carbon over. Nothing is gained and nothing is lost; the molecule is being put in a position where the next step can take a carbon off it.
The first CO₂. Six carbons become five, and this is the step the cycle is regulated at, because it is the first one that is hard to undo.
The first NADH. The point of the cycle is not the CO₂ leaving, it is the electrons being handed to NAD⁺ — those are what the electron transport chain spends to make ATP.
This complex is enormous, and it is the same architecture as the one that did pyruvate oxidation. Substrates never let go: a tether swings each intermediate to the next active site.
The second CO₂. Both carbons that came in as acetyl are now accounted for, and the molecule is back to four.
The second NADH, from the same step. Running the intermediates down a tether rather than releasing them is what keeps a reactive one from wandering off.
The bond to coenzyme A was holding energy, and breaking it pays for a nucleotide directly, with no membrane and no gradient involved.
GTP is ATP's near-twin and converts to it one-for-one. This is the cycle's ONLY direct fuel, one per turn, which is almost nothing beside the NADH.
The only step stuck in the membrane, because the enzyme doing it is also part of the electron transport chain. The cycle and the chain are literally the same protein here.
These electrons are too low in energy for NAD⁺, so they go to FAD instead and then straight into the membrane. Same idea, a cheaper carrier.
Coenzyme Q is small and greasy, so it dissolves in the bilayer and ferries electrons sideways through it.
Water adds across a double bond. Unremarkable chemistry, and it sets up the last step's oxidation.
The third NADH, and oxaloacetate is back. The molecule that started the turn has been rebuilt, and none of its atoms are the ones that left.
Ready for another acetyl-CoA. It is also raided for amino acids and nucleotides, so the cycle is a supply depot as much as a furnace.
Per turn: three NADH, one FADH₂, one GTP, two CO₂. Glucose gives two turns. The ATP is made later, by the chain those carriers feed.
